summary: Describes the Atom Publishing Protocol, an application-level protocol for publishing and editing web resources over HTTP using Atom-formatted representations. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: The Atom Publishing Protocol (AtomPub) uses Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) methods and Atom documents to create, read, edit, and delete web resources. Service documents describe collections, while servers control how they handle submitted content.

questions: what is the atom publishing protocol
how does atompub create a resource
what is a media link entry
subtitle: A small set of HTTP conventions for creating, editing and deleting web content using Atom feeds and entries.

tldr.problem: Clients such as blog editors needed a standard way to discover where they may publish and then create, change and remove web resources on a server.
tldr.mechanism: AtomPub uses plain HTTP: GET to read, POST to create, PUT to edit and DELETE to remove, with Atom documents describing resources, collections and what a server accepts.
tldr.outcome: It gives clients one protocol for publishing to many servers, while leaving servers wide latitude in how they treat submissions. It is a Proposed Standard, updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 5023 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2007 and has been updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What AtomPub Is
sections.content:
The Atom Publishing Protocol (AtomPub) is an application-level protocol for publishing and editing web resources. It runs over HTTP (RFC 2616) and XML 1.0, and uses Atom-formatted representations as defined in the Atom Syndication Format (RFC 4287).

It offers three facilities: Collections, which are sets of resources that can be retrieved in whole or in part; Services, for discovering and describing Collections; and Editing, for creating, editing and deleting resources.

A notable feature is that the server is given wide latitude. A server can accept, reject, delay, moderate, censor, reformat, translate, relocate or re-categorize what a client submits. So client software has to be written flexibly and accept whatever the server decides, and any server behaviour not explicitly forbidden by the RFC or HTTP is allowed.
sections.plainLanguage: AtomPub defines HTTP operations for publishing and editing web resources using Atom documents. A server may change or reject submitted content, so clients must handle different server responses.

sections.title: Resources, Collections and Service Documents
sections.content:
A resource whose IRI is listed in a Collection is a Member Resource. There are two kinds. An Entry Resource is represented as an Atom Entry Document. A Media Resource can have a representation in any media type, such as a picture, and is described in the Collection by an Entry called a Media Link Entry.

A Collection is represented as an Atom Feed whose Entries carry the IRIs of, and metadata about, the members. The RFC does not tell Collection Feeds apart from other Atom Feeds. The only signal is that the feed's IRI appears in a Service Document.

A Service Document groups Collections into named Workspaces. It tells a client the location of each Collection, which media types it accepts and which categories it allows. Workspaces have names but no IRIs and no specified processing model. How a client finds a Service Document is not defined by the RFC.

The RFC defines two document types in the http://www.w3.org/2007/app namespace: Category Documents (application/atomcat+xml) and Service Documents (application/atomsvc+xml). Unrecognized markup is treated as foreign markup: processors MUST NOT stop or signal an error, and clients SHOULD preserve it.
sections.plainLanguage: A Service Document lists Collections grouped into Workspaces and describes what each Collection accepts. A Collection feed lists resources, including entries that describe media files.

sections.title: Reading, Creating, Editing and Deleting
sections.content:
The protocol maps its operations onto four HTTP methods. GET retrieves a known resource, including a Service Document or a Collection feed. POST to the Collection URI creates a new, dynamically named resource. PUT edits a known resource and is not used for creation. DELETE removes one.

On a successful POST, the server answers 201 Created with a Location header holding the new Member Entry URI, and SHOULD return an Atom Entry Document in the body. The server is free to change the entry, for example the atom:id, so the returned copy helps the client line up its view with the server's. The client may treat the body as a complete representation only when a Content-Location header matches Location character for character. A collection may answer 415 Unsupported Media Type when it does not allow what was posted.

When editing, a client SHOULD preserve all metadata it did not mean to change, including unknown foreign markup. Deleting a Media Link Entry SHOULD delete the matching Media Resource. The status codes shown in the RFC's diagrams are examples; a client should be ready for any status code, since a PUT may return 204 No Content and still succeed.
sections.plainLanguage: GET reads a resource, POST creates one, PUT edits one, and DELETE removes one. After a successful POST, the server returns the new resource’s location.

sections.title: Media, Slugs, Paging and Drafts
sections.content:
When a client posts a non-Atom item, such as an image, the server MUST create two resources: the Media Resource and a Media Link Entry holding its metadata. The entry MUST have an atom:content element with a src attribute pointing at the media, and SHOULD carry an edit-media link for modifying it. The edit link relation marks an editable Member Entry, and an entry MUST NOT contain more than one.

The Slug header lets a client suggest text for the new resource's URI. Servers MAY use it for the last URI segment, the atom:id or the title, and MAY ignore or alter it. Its value is the percent-encoded UTF-8 form of the text.

Servers MAY return only a partial list of a Collection, ordered most recently edited first, with a next link to the following list and optionally previous, first and last links. Entries SHOULD carry one app:edited timestamp. A client may include app:draft with value yes inside app:control to ask that the item not be publicly visible; the server MAY ignore it, and absent the element it behaves as if no was sent. The RFC also adds a type parameter, entry or feed, to application/atom+xml.
sections.plainLanguage: A media upload creates both the media resource and an Atom entry that describes it. Clients can suggest a name with Slug or ask that an entry remain a draft, but the server may change or ignore those requests.

sections.title: Avoiding Lost Edits with Entity Tags
sections.content:
Implementers are advised to use HTTP cache controls and entity tags when editing, because clients are not assured of the most recent copy if the server lets intermediaries cache members.

The RFC walks through an example. The server returns an ETag when an entry is created. The client can later send it in If-None-Match on a GET, and gets 304 Not Modified if nothing changed. After editing, the client sends the tag in If-Match on the PUT. If the server has since received a newer copy, it answers 412 Precondition Failed and refuses to store the older edit.
sections.plainLanguage: Entity tags let a client check whether an entry has changed before replacing it. If another edit is newer, the server can reject the stale update with 412.

sections.title: Securing AtomPub
sections.content:
Authentication is RECOMMENDED but not required. Without it, clients and servers are open to trivial spoofing, denial-of-service and defacement attacks, although in some contexts that is an acceptable risk. The mechanism is a local decision, but at a minimum implementations MUST be capable of being configured to use HTTP Basic Authentication together with TLS 1.0 or a later standards-track version. Servers should answer unauthorized requests with an appropriate 4xx code such as 401 or 403.

The RFC lists further threats. Servers need to stop malicious clients from consuming excessive CPU, memory or disk. The protocol does not define a way to detect duplicate requests, so accidental duplicates look the same as replay attacks. Clients can send entries with inaccurate information anywhere. XML external entities and linked resources carry the usual network risks. Because servers may rewrite entries, a client's digital signature may not survive; the RFC recommends a server strip a signature it has invalidated. Finally, submitted content may carry code, so servers are strongly encouraged to verify that it is safe, with a white list working better than a black list for HTML.
sections.plainLanguage: Without authentication, another party may spoof requests or alter published content. Servers should limit resource use and check submitted content, while clients should treat linked resources and server changes carefully.
